hints: Look closely at what changes and what stays the same in the two structures.
Notice this is oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid, but a C=C double bond must survive untouched.
Think about which oxidising agent is gentle enough to oxidise -CHO but strong enough to break the C=C bond if conditions are too vigorous.
walkthrough:
**Identify the transformation**

Look at the functional groups. On the left you have an aldehyde, $-CHO$. On the right you have a carboxylic acid, $-COOH$. The cis $C=C$ bond is unchanged.

So we need: $$\text{R-CHO} \rightarrow \text{R-COOH}$$ while keeping $C=C$ intact.

**Recall aldehyde oxidation**

Aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids by mild oxidising agents with heating under reflux. The classic Cambridge reagent is acidified potassium dichromate(VI), $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}/\text{H}^+$.

**Protect the alkene**

The $C=C$ bond is very sensitive to strong oxidation. Hot, concentrated, acidified manganate(VII), $\text{MnO}_4^-/\text{H}^+$, will cleave the $C=C$ bond completely to give smaller fragments. Even dilute acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$ will attack the alkene.

Acidified dichromate(VI) will oxidise the aldehyde selectively and leave the $C=C$ alone under controlled reflux. Concentrated sulfuric acid is a dehydrating agent, not an oxidant for this change.

options.A: Acidified dichromate(VI) ions oxidise aldehydes to carboxylic acids on warming, but do not cleave isolated C=C bonds under these conditions. This gives exactly the required product with the cis alkene preserved.
options.B: Dilute, acidified manganate(VII) is still a very strong oxidant toward alkenes in acidic solution. Students often remember it as mild, but in acid it will attack the C=C bond as well as the aldehyde, so it will not give a clean product.
options.C: Hot, concentrated, acidified manganate(VII) is used for vigorous oxidative cleavage of C=C bonds. It would break the alkene chain into carboxylic acids, ketones and $\text{CO}_2$, destroying the starting carbon skeleton.
options.D: Concentrated sulfuric acid is a strong acid and dehydrating agent, not an oxidising agent for aldehydes. It would more likely cause dehydration, polymerisation or charring, not conversion of $-CHO$ to $-COOH$.
